debate.situation: You are the one who starts every plan with a friend. Time together is lovely, but if you stop texting, the contact stops. What you know is the pattern on your side; what you don't know is why your friend doesn't initiate, and that unknown decides whether this is a quiet imbalance, a difference in habits, or a friendship fading. The question underneath may be less whether to speak and more what you want the friendship to be.

minds.title: The Friendship Auditor
minds.concern: Whether goodwill and effort actually flow both ways, since a friendship is more than pleasant company.
minds.author: Aristotle

minds.title: The Plain Speaker
minds.concern: Saying what you observe, feel and need without turning it into an accusation.
minds.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg

minds.title: The Skeptic of Appearances
minds.concern: How quickly we build confident stories from the small slice of facts we can see.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

debate.speaker: The Friendship Auditor
debate.text: Say something. Lovely evenings prove you enjoy each other, not that the effort is shared. A friendship worth the name has goodwill running both ways. If you alone carry it, you may have a pleasant acquaintance who is happy to be carried.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Appearances
debate.text: You're judging from one data set: your own texts. You can't see what her silence means from inside her head. Maybe she assumes you like planning. Minds grab the facts in front of them and treat them as the whole story.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: You're both skipping a step. What happened is checkable: plans keep starting with your message. What it means is a guess. She doesn't care is an evaluation, not an observation. Start with the first, add how it feels, then make a concrete request.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Friendship Auditor
debate.text: Silence isn't a verdict, granted. But a pattern over time is evidence, and you can't know is a very comfortable place to hide forever. I'll narrow my claim: the pattern earns a question, not a conclusion about her.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Appearances
debate.text: Then watch the other trap: going quiet to see what happens. You'd read her silence as an answer using the same thin data. Worse, doing nothing is a real option. The evenings are lovely, the cost of texting is small.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: Agreed on the silent test: it's a punishment dressed as an experiment. But I'd also warn the Auditor that tallying effort turns a talk into an audit. And the motive is open. Hurt at feeling merely tolerated, tiredness from the workload, or a belief that friendships ought to be even each need a different conversation.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Appearances
debate.text: I doubt it's workload; she calls the evenings lovely. My bet is the fear of being tolerated. Still, that's a bet. The fact that reorders everything is why she doesn't start plans. Shy, swamped, content to be invited, or drifting: each points to a different move.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Friendship Auditor
debate.text: Then argue the branches. If she's simply unaware, one honest remark fixes it and the friendship deepens. If she knows and shrugs, you have a friendship of pleasure, which is real but lighter. Whether that's enough, or whether you'd rather have equality than ease, is yours to rank.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Plain Speaker
debate.text: And the speaking can be small. Mention that you've noticed you usually reach out first, say you'd love it if she picked the next plan, and ask if that works. It's a request, not a charge. Her answer, and what she does after, tells you more than any theory here.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Skeptic of Appearances
debate.text: I'll concede that much: waiting wins only if you never mind. If it nags you, silence isn't neutral, it's a decision to keep guessing. But one response won't settle it either. Give her time to act before you decide what her habits mean.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the choice isn't really speak versus stay quiet: the real alternatives are asking with curiosity, testing through silence, or accepting the rhythm as it is. What remains disputed is how much the pattern already says about her, and whether waiting is wise or just avoidance. A possible self-reflection: when this happens, is the feeling closer to being tolerated, being tired, or wanting things to be fair, and which of your wishes matters more, easy warmth or even effort?
debate.dependsOn: If it bothers you and the time together is genuinely good, a light, specific ask (could you pick the next plan?) becomes more reasonable, because it tests the pattern without accusing her. If it doesn't really bother you and you enjoy planning, continuing as you are becomes more reasonable, because the cost is small and the benefit real. If you ask and nothing changes over a while, you face a choice about what the friendship is worth to you as it stands. The decisive unknown is why she doesn't initiate; the proportionate way to learn it is the small request, and watching what she does with it.
